Bat
băt
n. (a flying creature of the night, listed with the unclean fowls; and, with the mole, the recipient of cast-away idols)
Middle English bakke, from a Scandinavian root. The Hebrew atalleph names the bat, which the law classes among the fowls because it flies, according to the ordinary way people speak rather than a modern taxonomy.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The bat closes both lists of unclean fowls: “And the stork, the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat” (Lev 11:19), and identically at Deuteronomy 14:18. It is the last name in a long catalogue, and the only creature in it that is not a bird. Isaiah gives it its great appearance: “In that day a man shall cast his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which they made each one for himself to worship, to the moles and to the bats” (Isa 2:20). Bats live in caves and ruined places, and the same chapter says men will go into the clefts of the rocks and into the tops of the ragged rocks for fear of the LORD; so the idols are flung into the very holes their owners are running toward. Isaiah elsewhere fills a judged land with such creatures — “the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it” (Isa 34:11). The birds of the dark inherit what proud men leave behind.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the bat as a quadruped of the genus Vespertilio, with wings formed of a membrane, which flies in the evening and lodges in caves and ruins.

expand to see more

BAT, n. An animal of the genus Vespertilio, having wings of membrane extended between the toes.

It flies in the twilight and night, and lodges by day in caverns and old buildings.

The lapwing, and the bat. Lev. xi.

BAT, n. A heavy stick or club; a piece of wood with one end thicker than the other.

Key Scripture

Lev 11:19 — "And the stork, the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat."

Deu 14:18 — "And the stork, and the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat."

Isa 2:20 — "In that day a man shall cast his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which they made each one for himself to worship, to the moles and to the bats;"

Isa 34:11 — "But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness."

Modern Corruption

That Leviticus classes the bat with fowls is offered as proof of biblical error, though the text is using ordinary speech about flying creatures, not a modern taxonomy.

expand to see more

The bat is a standing exhibit in the argument that the Bible contains scientific mistakes: it is a mammal, and Leviticus lists it among the fowls. The objection assumes that the chapter is offering a classification of the animal kingdom by descent and physiology, which is a category invented in the eighteenth century and later. The Hebrew word rendered fowl is oph, from a root meaning to fly, and it means simply the flying things — a functional grouping, exactly as an English speaker still calls a whale a sea creature or speaks of the sun rising. Leviticus 11:20 makes the same functional move with insects, speaking of fowls that creep, going upon all four. Scripture is inerrant in what it asserts, and it asserts here which creatures Israel may eat, in the ordinary language of the people who had to obey it.

Isaiah's use of the bat is where the entry earns its keep. The idols of silver and gold were made each one for himself to worship — commissioned, paid for, and known to be manufactured — and in the day of the LORD's terror they are thrown to the bats and moles while their owners scramble into the rocks. That is not a picture of men repenting; it is a picture of men discarding. There is a moment, and Scripture insists it is coming, when every substitute for God is instantly and universally seen to be worthless, and the seeing will not save anybody who waited for it. The gospel calls men to make the same judgment now, while it can be made with a whole heart: turn from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew atalleph (H5847), a bat; with oph (H5775), a flying thing, the functional category of the list, and elil (H457), an idol.

expand to see more

Hebrew atalleph (H5847) — a bat; last named in both lists of unclean fowls; Leviticus 11:19, Deuteronomy 14:18.

Hebrew oph (H5775) — a flying creature, from uph, to fly; the functional category rendered fowl.

Hebrew chapharperah (H2661) — a mole, a digger; named with the bat as recipient of the idols; Isaiah 2:20.

Hebrew elil (H457) — an idol, a thing of nought; Isaiah 2:20, Psalm 96:5.

Hebrew tohu (H8414) — confusion, emptiness; the line of confusion stretched over a judged land; Isaiah 34:11.

Usage

"“The lapwing, and the bat” — last in the list, and the only one that is not a bird."

"“To the moles and to the bats” — silver gods thrown into the dark."

"“The owl also and the raven shall dwell in it” — who inherits what pride leaves."
